The rate limit sits in another file, so this file cannot show it is working.
The secret rules are enforced in the settings loader, not here.

terms.meaning: The record that says who is signed in, kept between requests.
A token that holds session data and is signed so it cannot be changed without detection.
A sign-in method that checks an email and password the user types in.
A cap on how often one client can try, to slow down guessing.
The network address that identifies the device making a request.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Sign-in setup and types
sections.what: Declares that a session includes a user id, and brings in the sign-in provider, the credential checker, the client address helper and the settings reader.
sections.why: Lets the rest of the app read the user id from a session without type errors.
sections.watch_out: The type declaration must stay in place, or code that reads the user id will not type check.

sections.name: sessionSecret
sections.title: Signing key for sessions
sections.what: Reads the secret used to sign sessions from the settings.
sections.why: Signing stops anyone forging a session token.
sections.watch_out: Changing this secret signs every user out, and the minimum length rule is enforced in the settings loader, not here.

sections.name: authOptions
sections.title: Email and password sign-in
sections.what: Configures sign-in with email and password, which calls the credential checker with the client address. Stores the user id in a signed token, sends sign-in to /login, and keeps no session table in the database.
sections.why: Likely reason: a signed token avoids a database lookup on every request.
sections.watch_out: The rate limit is applied inside the credential checker, so changing that code changes sign-in protection without any change here.

summary: The sign-in setup: users sign in with email and password, and a signed token keeps them signed in.
purpose: It lets people sign in to the app and tells the rest of the app who they are.
why: Likely reason: a signed token keeps sessions working without a database lookup on every request.
how: It declares that sessions carry a user id, builds the signing secret, and configures the email and password provider. The provider checks the password and applies a rate limit by client address. The user id is copied into the token and the session, and sign-in is sent to the /login page.
inputs: The email, password and client address from the sign-in form, plus the signing secret from the settings.
outputs: A signed session for a valid sign-in, or a failed sign-in.
risks: Changing the signing secret signs every user out. Sign-in protection lives in another file, so changing that file changes this behaviour.
debug: If sign-in fails, check the rate limit message and the credential check. If users are signed out unexpectedly, check that the signing secret has not changed.
